blocks.title: Five capitals are not five equal governments
paragraphs: Historical accounts describe Balhae's network of five capitals, fifteen prefectures and sixty-two subprefectures or provinces in forms derived largely from Chinese dynastic compilations. These figures are useful but should not be converted uncritically into a comprehensive contemporary census of functioning offices. The Academy of Korean Studies notes uncertainty about when the mature arrangement was completed, commonly placing its establishment by the early ninth century.

A central court could use a primary seat of monarchy while other capitals served as administrative, strategic or symbolic hubs. Relative importance changed with royal movements and surrounding economic conditions. The network was a tool for integrating dispersed spaces, not evidence that every capital exercised identical authority. Maps are reconstructed from historical place names and excavated settlements, and disputed identifications remain part of the scholarly record.

blocks.title: Sanggyeong and the built form of kingship
paragraphs: Sanggyeong Yongcheonbu, often associated with the Shangjing Longquanfu site near modern Ning'an, displays the significance of a planned metropolitan centre. Large structural foundations, street alignments, roof tiles and palace areas reflect the concentration of labour and material resources around the court. The resemblance to Tang-style urban planning demonstrates cultural exchange without making the city a mere copy of Chang'an.

Monumental construction required sustained political capacity: artisans, transport, timber, fired tiles, food and workers. Architectural remains can demonstrate planned building, but cannot tell how every suburb was populated or which classes lived along each street. Nor should one restored map be presented as a flawless photograph of the eighth century. The city's material history continued through multiple reigns and should be separated from legends about one ruler's original intention.

evidence.claim: The Academy of Korean Studies discusses five capitals and fifteen prefectures within a debated chronology.

blocks.title: Prefectures and indirect governance
paragraphs: The fifteen bu formed important regional nodes below the royal centre. Textual accounts associate them with subordinate ju and other administrative units, but local circumstances varied. Some areas contained long-standing communities and leaders who could mediate the king's demands. A district's formal classification need not mean officials sent from the capital supervised every household continuously.

The distinction between an appointed governor and a chief incorporated into a royal hierarchy matters for explaining Balhae's territorial reach. A court might collect goods or mobilize troops through an existing local leader while retaining less control over everyday disputes. Documentary gaps make it hard to determine the proportion of direct and indirect administration. Regional archaeology and the careful mapping of offices provide evidence for competing interpretations, not a simple test of whether a place belonged to Balhae.
blocks.label: Original historical synthesis

blocks.title: Roads made administration possible
paragraphs: Cities and prefectural centres depended on practical connections: land routes through difficult terrain, navigable rivers and passages toward neighboring courts. A journey between capitals involved provisions, guides, secure stops and coordination among regions. The existence of named routes in historical texts can identify corridors of significance but does not prove a uniformly maintained road surface for the whole distance.

Transport infrastructure also shaped the limits of military power. An army could cross a boundary on a campaign without a court retaining the ability to deliver orders and collect resources each season. Such logistical constraints help explain why Balhae could be territorially extensive yet administratively uneven. The central challenge was making political claims effective across varied ecology and distance.
blocks.label: Original historical synthesis

blocks.title: Territorial maps and the problem of precision
paragraphs: Maps of Balhae commonly cover large areas of today's northeastern China and the Russian Far East, in addition to northern parts of the peninsula. Boundaries are difficult to establish precisely, partly because evidence for population, administrative naming and temporary military influence is not equivalent. Scholarly debates concern the locations of particular prefectures and the extent of royal control in borderland districts.

The figures five, fifteen and sixty-two themselves demand source criticism: the received New Book of Tang lists sixty named ju although it reports a total of sixty-two. Treating the difference as an embarrassment to conceal would deprive readers of an excellent example of the limitations of transmitted geography. Scholars use later geographical works, inscriptions and excavation to evaluate identifications. Where evidence remains insufficient, a hatched frontier is more faithful than a confidently drawn line.
blocks.label: Original historical synthesis

blocks.title: Administration across cultural differences
paragraphs: Balhae's territory brought communities with varying languages, economic patterns and historical relationships under claims of royal authority. Local administration necessarily involved negotiation, but texts usually record those relationships from the viewpoint of court-centred institutions. We cannot reconstruct a uniform policy toward every community based simply on a list of prefectures.

Different forms of rule were compatible within one kingdom. In some regions, court officials may have monitored agriculture and transport; in others, ties of allegiance, tribute and military support may have been more important. This is not proof that the kingdom was fragile or incoherent. Large premodern states often governed unevenly. The evidence invites examination of how political expectations were translated through existing local leadership rather than a binary judgment of complete sovereignty versus no sovereignty.
blocks.label: Original historical synthesis

blocks.title: Reading the number sixty-two critically
paragraphs: The figure of sixty-two ju appears repeatedly in summaries of Balhae's administrative system. It is memorable and provides a framework for understanding the scale of government. Yet the received New Book of Tang account includes a discrepancy between its stated total and the number of subordinate names it preserves. The Academy of Korean Studies specifically notes that sixty names are listed. The difference has led researchers to compare other geographical sources and propose additional identifications.

This is not a trivial numerical puzzle. An administrative map built from such a list may locate an official name confidently while leaving its position or even its continued operation uncertain. Names can change, duplicate other place names, or be transmitted with copying errors. Archaeological evidence of a fortified or planned settlement may suggest a major district, but the attribution of a named office requires corroboration.

The most precise history does not merely reproduce the five/fifteen/sixty-two formula. It explains what each tier meant in surviving court descriptions, how a capital functioned differently from an ordinary prefectural seat, and which parts of the geography are hypotheses. Distinguishing formal hierarchy from local rule also helps explain Balhae's breadth: administrative design was a way to coordinate regional groups, not proof that every locality was governed identically at all times.

blocks.title: What a provincial office could actually do
paragraphs: The word prefecture can imply a standing bureaucracy with regular territorial jurisdiction. For Balhae it is more cautious to identify a named administrative unit and then ask how its officials secured resources and obedience. A provincial commander or governor needed clerks, reliable messengers, storage facilities and some means of translating central orders into locally intelligible demands. A court's creation of a title did not guarantee all these capacities at once. The scale of surviving evidence differs considerably across the region.

Where archaeology has found planned centres, roof tiles, compounds or fortifications, the material basis for organized authority becomes more visible. But naming one site as the seat of an office requires careful correlation between excavated strata and transmitted geography. A fortification might predate or outlast the administrative designation assigned to it. Monumental architecture can indicate political investment without identifying the daily power of the people living nearby. The test is whether different classes of evidence point toward the same chronological reconstruction.

The province was also inhabited by people whose lives could not be contained in royal decrees. Agricultural communities, forest groups and inhabitants of transport corridors might relate to officials through different obligations. Some would experience demands for goods and labour more directly, while others may have dealt principally with chiefs or intermediaries. Balhae's administrative achievement was the integration of these relationships within a wide political network. It did not require social homogeneity, and the historian should not make administrative vocabulary a substitute for describing local agency.

The ability to maintain capitals and routes across several centuries demonstrates real coordination. Still, such networks were vulnerable to war, changes in alliance and interruptions of supply. The range between the ambitious formal geography recorded in later sources and the uneven practice of local government is precisely where many important historical questions lie. The debate over sixty-two listed units is one example of a broader evidential challenge rather than the sole uncertainty in the map.
